newsitem.title: JORDAN: Two Jordanian papers on hold after new press law.
newsitem.headline: Two Jordanian papers on hold after new press law.

text.p: Two Jordanian weekly newspapers said on Thursday they were suspending publication in response to restrictions imposed under an amended press law.

One paper said it was halting its printing presses for a month while it tried to meet the law's new capital requirements. The other said it would be off the streets for three weeks in protest at the law.

Al-Mithaq weekly's editor Nahed Hattar said his paper, which has a circulation of 16,000, would try to raise the 300,000 dinar ($423,000) capital requirement by mid-August. If it failed it would fold, he said.
"This is the aim of the government, to shut us down," Hattar told Reuters.
He said his paper was also being taken to court over an article, written since the law was issued, criticising the political situation in Jordan.
The revised law set wideranging restrictions on reporting and raised minimum fines for offenders to 15,000 dinars from 1,000 dinars.

The Jordanian al-Hayat newspaper's managing director Daygham Khreisat said his paper, with a circulation of 20,000, could meet the capital requirements but was threatened by the higher fines and was suspending publication for a limited period in protest.
"Two or three court cases could force a weekly paper to close," he said.
If the newspapers shut down they will follow the satirical weekly Abed Rebbo, which closed last month saying it could no longer afford to publish in Jordan.
A group of five newspapers are appealing against the law in the courts, saying it was issued unconstitutionally by the government without being referred to parliament.
They say the expect a ruling on their appeal next month.
Journalists say most of Jordan's numerous weekly papers, many of which are opposition-leaning and have only a modest circulation, will be forced to close unless the new press law is amended.
